lesson.1_1.title: Income, expenses, needs and wants
lesson.1_1.gut.prompt: It's Month 1. Your family covers food, school fees and travel. You have ₹2,000 to use however you like. A pair of sneakers you love costs ₹1,800. What do you do?
lesson.1_1.gut.a.label: Buy the sneakers
lesson.1_1.gut.a.result: You have the sneakers and ₹200 left. Next month a friend asks you to a movie: you have ₹200. Joy now, but little room for anything else.
lesson.1_1.gut.b.label: Save all ₹2,000
lesson.1_1.gut.b.result: You have ₹2,000 saved. Nothing to spend on a friend's movie, and no new shoes. Safe, but a little dull.
lesson.1_1.gut.c.label: Split: ₹1,200 save, ₹800 spend
lesson.1_1.gut.c.result: You can enjoy something small and still grow your savings. Nice balance.
lesson.1_1.gut.bridge: There's no single right answer. Let's learn the words that help you decide.
lesson.1_1.c1.text: Money comes in. Money goes out. Where does yours go?
lesson.1_1.c2.text: Income is money that comes to you. Pocket money, a gift, a part-time job, a scholarship.
lesson.1_1.c3.text: An expense is money you spend. Some come every month, like a phone recharge. Some come now and then, like a birthday gift.
lesson.1_1.c4.text: Fixed expenses stay the same: bus pass, tuition fee. Variable expenses change: snacks, outings.
lesson.1_1.c4.reveal.prompt: Which one can you change more easily?
lesson.1_1.c4.reveal.answer: Variable expenses. You choose how many snacks and outings.
lesson.1_1.c5.text: A need is something you must have to live and study. A want is something that makes life nicer, but you can live without it.
lesson.1_1.c6.text: Some things are in between. A phone for studying is a need. An ₹80,000 phone is more of a want. Ask: "What happens if I don't buy this?"
lesson.1_1.c6.sort.prompt: Sort each one: need or want?
lesson.1_1.c6.sort.feedback: Needs keep you living and studying. Wants make life nicer. Both are fine; wants just need a plan.
lesson.1_1.c7.text: In Capito, your needs are already covered by your family or by you. The money you earn here is only for wants and savings.
lesson.1_1.c7.footer: Wants are not bad. They just need a plan.
lesson.1_1.c8.text: ₹40 a day on snacks sounds small. In a year it's ₹14,600.
lesson.1_1.q1.prompt: Which of these is a want?
lesson.1_1.q1.right: Yes. The skin is nice, but you can live without it. That makes it a want.
lesson.1_1.q1.wrong: Fees, rice and a bus pass are things you need to live and study. The skin is nice, but you can live without it.
lesson.1_1.q2.prompt: You spend ₹40 on snacks every day. About how much is that in a year?
lesson.1_1.q2.right: Right: ₹40 × 365 days = ₹14,600. Small spends add up.
lesson.1_1.q2.wrong: Multiply ₹40 by 365 days. Small spends add up to ₹14,600.
lesson.1_1.q3.prompt: Spending on wants is always a bad thing.
lesson.1_1.q3.right: Correct, it's false. Wants are part of a good life. The skill is planning for them.
lesson.1_1.q3.wrong: It's false. Wants are part of a good life. The skill is planning for them, so they don't crowd out your savings.
lesson.1_1.effect: Your Month 1 money lands in your Wallet, and you add your first want to My Wants.
lesson.1_2.title: Turn wants into goals
lesson.1_2.gut.prompt: A friend asks you to join a ₹1,200 trip in 2 months. You are saving for a ₹3,000 laptop bag. What do you do?
lesson.1_2.gut.bridge: A want with a price and a date becomes a goal. Here's how to plan one.
lesson.1_2.gut.a.label: Go on the trip, pause the bag
lesson.1_2.gut.a.result: A fun trip with friends. The bag now arrives about 2 months later than you planned.
lesson.1_2.gut.b.label: Skip the trip, keep saving
lesson.1_2.gut.b.result: The bag arrives on time, but you miss a day out with your friends.
lesson.1_2.gut.c.label: Plan for both
lesson.1_2.gut.c.result: You save ₹600 a month for the trip, then go back to the bag. Both happen, the bag a little later.
lesson.1_2.c1.text: A want is a wish. A goal is a wish with a price and a date.
lesson.1_2.c2.text: A goal has three parts: what it is, how much it costs, and by when. "Headphones, ₹1,500, by Month 5" is a goal.
lesson.1_2.c2.reveal.prompt: Which one is a goal: "I want new shoes" or "Shoes, ₹1,800, by Month 6"?
lesson.1_2.c2.reveal.answer: The second one. It has a price and a date, so you can plan for it.
lesson.1_2.c3.text: Some goals are close, some are far. Short-term goals come within months. Medium-term goals take a year or two. Long-term goals are years away.
lesson.1_2.c3.sort.prompt: How far away is each goal?
lesson.1_2.c3.sort.feedback: Short goals are near, long goals are years away. Most people have a mix of both.
lesson.1_2.c4.text: To reach a goal, divide the price by the months you have. ₹3,000 in 6 months is ₹500 a month.
lesson.1_2.c5.text: Starting late makes each month harder. ₹3,000 in 3 months is ₹1,000 a month, twice as much.
lesson.1_2.c6.text: Every rupee can be spent only once. The ₹1,200 you spend on a trip can't also go to your bag. That trade-off is called opportunity cost.
lesson.1_2.c7.text: You can add, change or drop goals any time. Life changes, and so can your plan.
lesson.1_2.c7.footer: In this game you set three starter goals now.
lesson.1_2.q1.prompt: Which of these is a goal?
lesson.1_2.q1.right: Yes. It has a thing, a price and a date, so you can plan for it.
lesson.1_2.q1.wrong: A goal needs a price and a date. "Earbuds, ₹1,500, by Month 5" has both.
lesson.1_2.q2.prompt: You want ₹3,000 in 6 months. How much should you put aside each month?
lesson.1_2.q2.wrong: Divide the price by the months: ₹3,000 ÷ 6 = ₹500 a month.
lesson.1_2.q3.prompt: Spending ₹1,200 on a trip has no effect on your other goals.
lesson.1_2.q3.right: Correct, it's false. That ₹1,200 can't also go to your other goals. That's opportunity cost.
lesson.1_2.q3.wrong: It's false. Money spent on one thing can't go to another, so other goals move back. That's opportunity cost.
lesson.1_2.effect: Set three starter goals. Each month you can put money towards them and watch the progress bars fill.
lesson.1_3.title: The budget: pay yourself first
lesson.1_3.gut.prompt: ₹4,000 arrives this month. Do you spend first and save what's left, or save first and spend the rest?
lesson.1_3.gut.bridge: Saving first is a habit called "pay yourself first". A budget makes it easy.
lesson.1_3.gut.a.label: Spend first, save what's left
lesson.1_3.gut.a.result: By the end of the month only ₹200 is left to save. Three months like this: ₹600 saved.
lesson.1_3.gut.b.label: Save ₹1,600 first, spend the rest
lesson.1_3.gut.b.result: ₹2,400 still goes to your wants. Three months like this: ₹4,800 saved.
lesson.1_3.gut.c.label: Save all of it
lesson.1_3.gut.c.result: ₹12,000 saved in three months, but no fun at all. That's hard to keep up.
lesson.1_3.c1.text: A budget is a plan for your money, made before you spend it.
lesson.1_3.c2.text: The simple version: Income − Savings = Spending. Decide the savings part first, then spend what is left. That's pay yourself first.
lesson.1_3.c3.text: A popular guide is 50-30-20: about 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings.
lesson.1_3.c4.text: In Capito your needs are already covered. So the 30 and the 20 become 60% wants and 40% savings of your practice money.
lesson.1_3.c5.text: Your savings rate is the share of your money that you save. Saving ₹1,600 out of ₹4,000 is a 40% savings rate.
lesson.1_3.c6.text: It's a guide, not a rule. Change it to fit your life. Even ₹100 saved first, every month, builds the habit.
lesson.1_3.c7.text: Keep track of where money goes: a notebook, your UPI history, or one envelope for each part of the plan. Try a budget now.
lesson.1_3.q1.o1: Save whatever is left at the end of the month
lesson.1_3.q1.o2: Put your savings aside as soon as money arrives
lesson.1_3.q1.o3: Spend on wants first, then think about saving
lesson.1_3.q1.right: Yes. Savings come out first, then you spend the rest without worry.
lesson.1_3.q1.wrong: Pay yourself first means savings come out as soon as money arrives. Waiting for leftovers usually leaves little.
lesson.1_3.q2.prompt: With the game's 60/40 split, how much of ₹4,000 goes to savings?
lesson.1_3.q2.right: Right: 40% of ₹4,000 is ₹1,600. The other ₹2,400 is for wants.
lesson.1_3.q2.wrong: 40% of ₹4,000 is ₹1,600. ₹2,400 is the wants part.
lesson.1_3.q3.prompt: Having a budget means you can never spend on wants.
lesson.1_3.q3.right: Correct, it's false. A budget plans for wants too, so you can enjoy them without guilt.
lesson.1_3.q3.wrong: It's false. A good budget has room for wants. It just decides the savings part first.
lesson.1_3.effect: Plan the Month now suggests a 60/40 split of your money, and your savings rate starts counting towards your Money Health Score.
lesson.1_4.title: Assets, liabilities and net worth
lesson.1_4.gut.prompt: You can buy a ₹6,000 phone, or put ₹6,000 in a savings account. One year later, which is worth more?
lesson.1_4.gut.bridge: Some things you own grow, some shrink. Let's name them.
lesson.1_4.gut.a.label: The phone
lesson.1_4.gut.a.result: After a year the phone is worth about ₹4,200. You did get to use it every day.
lesson.1_4.gut.b.label: The savings account
lesson.1_4.gut.b.result: About ₹6,180 after a year at 3%. Safe and growing a little, but no new phone.
lesson.1_4.gut.c.label: They are worth the same
lesson.1_4.gut.c.result: Not quite. The phone loses value as it gets older, while the savings earn a little interest.
lesson.1_4.c1.text: Everything you own has a value. Everything you owe counts too.
lesson.1_4.c2.text: An asset is something you own that has value: money in savings, a cycle, gold earrings.
lesson.1_4.c3.text: A liability is money you owe: a loan, an EMI still to pay, money borrowed from a friend.
lesson.1_4.c3.sort.feedback: Assets are what you own. Liabilities are what you owe.
lesson.1_4.c3.sort.phoneLoan: A phone loan you are still repaying
lesson.1_4.c4.text: Net worth = assets − liabilities. Own ₹60,000 and owe ₹10,000? Your net worth is ₹50,000.
lesson.1_4.c5.text: Many things lose value as they get older. That's depreciation. A ₹6,000 phone that loses 30% a year is worth about ₹5,020 after 6 months.
lesson.1_4.c6.text: Other things can hold or grow their value, like savings that earn interest. Nothing is guaranteed, but it helps to know which is which.
lesson.1_4.c7.text: Buying a phone on EMI means paying interest on something that is losing value. Worth a thought before you buy.
lesson.1_4.q1.right: Yes. A loan is money you owe, so it's a liability.
lesson.1_4.q1.wrong: Savings and a bicycle are things you own. A loan is money you owe, so it's the liability.
lesson.1_4.q2.prompt: You own things worth ₹20,000 and owe ₹5,000. What is your net worth?
lesson.1_4.q2.wrong: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe: ₹20,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹15,000.
lesson.1_4.q3.prompt: A new phone usually keeps its full price for years.
lesson.1_4.q3.right: Correct, it's false. Phones lose value as they get older. That's depreciation.
lesson.1_4.q3.wrong: It's false. Phones lose value every month. That's called depreciation.
lesson.1_4.effect: Your net-worth card goes live. Anything you buy from your wants shows up in Things I own and loses a little value each month.
